definition.text: A stormwater fee charges property owners for polluted rainwater runoff from their hard, waterproof surfaces.

facts.text: The charge grows with the area of roofs, driveways and paving that stop rain soaking into the ground.
In Germany builders install rain storage tanks and soakaways to lower the fee, raising rainwater recycling and cutting tap water use.
A 2023 study counted at least 2,100 stormwater utilities in 42 US states and the District of Columbia.
Maryland's 2012 fee, dubbed a 'rain tax', funded runoff controls to clean up the Chesapeake Bay but was made optional in 2015.

title: Tax incidence

definition.text: Tax incidence describes who actually ends up paying a tax, which may differ from who hands the money to the government.

facts.text: If a 10% tax on butter sellers raises the market price by 8%, then 80% of the burden falls on buyers.
The steeper the demand curve and the flatter the supply curve, the more consumers bear the tax; the reverse puts it on producers.
Most markets lie between these extremes, so producers and consumers share the burden.
Ultimately every tax falls on people: owners, customers or workers.
The full burden of a tax includes lost consumer and producer surplus, not just the money collected.

contested_note: Public finance economists disagree greatly on how far market forces shift the burden of particular taxes.

definition.text: A tax shift, or tax swap, cuts some taxes and raises others while keeping total revenue the same.

facts.text: It can mean a desired move toward socially efficient taxes such as ecotaxes and sin taxes.
A green tax shift raises taxes on pollution while lowering taxes such as income, payroll or property taxes.
Its aim is often 'full cost accounting', using fiscal policy to fold externalities into prices.
Tax shifts usually aim to stay revenue-neutral and keep the system progressive, protecting the most vulnerable.
British Columbia's carbon tax shift gave it one of Canada's lowest income tax rates as of 2012.

definition.text: A user fee is a payment charged to people for using a facility or service, such as a park, toll road or parking space.

facts.text: Fuel taxes that fund highways act as user fees: those who drive more pay more for roads.
Unlike broad taxes, user fees fall only on those who use the service.
Critics argue that fees for basic services in developing countries hurt the poorest most.
